T is not always so easy to get rid of

Too much even of genuine wit is cloy¬

veare, anchovies, and Dutch herrings,

Let us first lay a so undation of good beef

or mutton, if you please : for. there is

no living upon pickles op sweet-meat$

alone.

The ground-work of every perform¬

ance, even of those which admit or re¬

quire the greatest profufion of orna¬

ments, ought to be plain and Ample.

Observe Nature : in the meadow, the

sweet green, yrhich never dazzles the

fight, is the predominant colour;

while the gaudy flowers, red, white,

yellow, blue, and purple, are careiefsly

interspersed. This is inflnitly more

pleaflng and beautiful than that inflpid,

childifli, uncomfortable bauble called

a flower-knot ; and the wild variety of the woods as far excels the richefi: plan¬

tation of flowering flirubs. I would not

be above taking a hint even from the

mechanic arts : if a fu;t of cloaths is

overcharged with lace, it become^

tawdry and ungenteel. In every work,

the true tafle is to dispose the ornaments

with esfe and propriety, and not to be

upon your performance an elegant rich-

nels, and such a modefl: dignity as will

please every true eye; though it may

don: for they are sometimes in raptures,

Essay on Tragedy and Comedy.

TWTOtwithstanding the opinion of

JL'% fame old critic, that a perfect

tragedy is the noblest production of which the human wit is capable 5 it

has long been a subject of learned

dispute, whether a perfect comedy was

not the more difficult undertaking of the two. The great majority of judges,

who are not always in the right, have

I believe Hill given the preference to

comedy in this respect. They tell

you that as comedy is a representation

of common life, and incidents that

are exposed to daily observation, if

must be a work of more difficult exe¬

cution : since most people truely are

qualified to judge of what is na¬

tural in common life. But are we

not equally judges of natural expref-

fions in cafes of the most tragical dif-

tress ? Even in the most exalted person-

ages ? What should hinder ? Do the

passions operate differently in similar

lltuations according to the different-

ranks of mankind ? A king or an em¬

peror may upon occasion be as much

enraged as a chafed dray-man 5 only

he’ll express his anger with mare dig¬

nity and in more decent language.

It. is, no doubt, equally the business

of tragedy and comedy to represent

life and characters naturally. And we

have as good a right to expect true pic¬

tures of nature from the one as from the other.

Mean time, I imagine the working up of a good tragedy to be by many

degrees the more difficult and arduous

talk of the two. Except you think the

sublime productions of Raphael required

less

less genius than those of Hogarth 5

whom I would never be understood to

mention but in terms of great esteem

and admiration. How many tolerable

comedies have we seen for one trage¬

dy, in which the passions are fiaturally

represented, and expreft with propriety

and spirit ? Mouthing, big words, tur¬

gid unnatural language, and affected

sentiments, are nothing to the pur-

pose; indeed of moving the passions,

they only create contempt and disgust

in people of proper feelings. I would

afk how many very good comic ro¬

mances have appeared in the European

languages for one tolerable epic poem ?

Let me afk. again, how many excel¬

lent comedians of both sexes have ap¬

peared upon the English stage within the memory of many now living, for

one that has excelled in tragedy ?

As to what Moliere fays upon this

subject, I think it is in his Critique

de l’Ecoie des Femmes, it amounts to

no more than this 5 that it is much

easier to write a bad tragedy than a

good comedy; which I suppose will

be readily granted.

After all, I believe it must be allow¬

ed, that a loud ranting declamatory

tragedy, in which nature is perpetual¬

ly kept at the truncheon’s end 5 with the assistance especially of magnificent

dreffes, changes of amusing feenes, al¬

tars, sacrifices, processions, public au¬

diences of ambafiadors, and such other

troduced ; is much more likely to im-

pose upon the eyes and ears of the

multitude than a cold insipid comedy.

The Motives.

Their motives for engaging in a war

The Elephant

Is the largest quadrupede in the

world, being foraetimes fifteen feet

high, and thick in proportion. It is,

however, an animal too well known to

admit of a minute description at this

period. Yet may some few of its pro¬

perties be less familiar than its figure.

The only part of the elephant used in

medicine, is the tooth, known all over

‘England by the name of ivory. It has

indeed much the fame virtue ac harts¬

horn, and may be prepared in the fame

manner.

Som e pretend it will cure the jaundice,

kill worms, ease pain, strengthen the

ilomach, and abate the fits of au epi-

lepfy, but without any just foundation.

When they are wild, they always go

in herds, the largest foremost; and when they are to cross a river, they lift up the

young ones with their tuiks, and twist

their trunk round the middle. There

are different methods of taking wild

elephants; one of which is, to dig a

pit, and cover it with boughs and

grafs, that the besft may fall into it, as

he passes along. Another is, to drive

them into a narrow place made so

strong with polls and rails, that they

cannot get out of it; and then they

employ the tame elephants to bring

them to reason. Two of them will get

a wild one between them, and beat him

with their trunks till they have made

him quite tame. If, after this, he re-

fufes to do as h$ is bid, they make

signs to the tame ones, who immediately

cor rest him, and oblige the poor animal

to obey. , )

a. The kiftg cannot by his prerogative vary

not go beyond the letter of the law in point of

CASE.

A man convicted for felony without bene¬

fit of clergy, receives sentence in court in the words following, viz. <c That you be taken

hence to the place from whence you came, and from thence to the usual place of execution

where you are to be hanged by the neck until

you are dead.”

For the executing of this fame man, the fol¬

lowing is fent by the recorder:

London T To the sheriffs of the city of

and > London and to the sheriff of

MLddlesex. j the county of Middlesex, and to the keeper of his maiefty’s

gaol of Newgate.

WHEREAS at the session of gaol deli¬

very of Newgate for the city of London and county of Middlesex, holden at Justice-Hali-

in the Old Bailey on the of

last, A. B. received sentence of death for his

offence in the indictment against him men¬

tioned : and whereas it has been duly signihed

to me that it is his majesty’s pleasure that the

livid sentence be executed in the most convenient

place near Bethnal-Green church, in the coun¬

Given under my hand and seal this day of 1769.

James Eyr e, Recorder.

Your opinion is Tj fired, whether a sheriff

will by law be 3uftifed in executing such war¬

rant of the recorder ?

Mr. Serjeant Glynn s opinion.

I confess a very great difficulty in answering

this question. If the place is a material part of

sentence, the omission of which would vi¬

tiate the judgement, the execution must be con¬

formable to it, and I know no authority that

Talline* 39

can justify a deviation from it. The "king may

pardon all or part of the sentence, hut cannot

alter, it; the sherifPs authority is the sentence,

he is bound to lopk to it, and fee it rightly ex¬

ecuted. If the placq is not material, then I

should conceive it to be in the sheriff’s difere-

tion, he being responsible for the fitness and

propriety of the place. I know not how to ac¬

count fer the many instances of execution in

places different from the judgement by com¬

mand of the judges upon the circuit, or his majesty in London and Middlesex, than as re¬

commendations to die sheriffs and intended in¬

demnities to them against the consequences of

departing from ancient usage. There are certain

cafes in which the sheriffs must disobey such

commands, viz. if the crown commanded an

execution in a private room or a church, &c.

Though I am not determined in my judgement

with respedt to the materiality of the place in

the sentence, I have no doubt of the conclusion

that must follow from either proposftion : if it

is material, no power can change it; if it i#

not material, the sheriff is intrusted with the

execution of the sentence, and must have it in

his power to judge of the place, I should ad-

vife the sheriffs to represent to his majesty the

doubts conceived bv them: the more so as I

J /

cannot but doubt of the propriety of signifying his majesty’s pleasure through the recorder,

being much inclined to think that the sheriffs

cannot in any case be justifted but by the com¬

mands of the king or the court directed ta

them.

Nov. 13, 1769. John Glynn,

This is an important subject and deferyes'

what it was when i.t lay open j but then it i-s

observed, that fewer hands are required to ma¬

natural consequence is certainly advantageous

•to the publick as well as individuals, A -great¬

er abundance of corn or cattle can never be ere-

maintain its ground, especially in a country

like England ; for tillage (except in some few

articles) is far from being so preferable to gra¬

zings as is commonly pretended, on account of

employing a superior number of hands. Ao.

exact enquiry into circuniftaricesj, at leaf! in a

nation risen to grandeur, opulent and luxuri¬

ous, w$l perhaps prove the contrary,—Let it

that the proportion of hands in the different

one.. This superiority ran ft be p resumed n.e-

.ceiTary for plowing, lowing, reaping, th re fil¬

ing, in short for the whole country bufintffh

requisite ,to prepare the grain for the miller or

maltster : the baker, brewer, or difiilkr, are

all that follow, as persons employed in a fur¬

ther preparation of it for the consumer. And

here ends the benefit of corn to society in the

way of employing its members. But in grazing,

the Angle article of wool qlone, the produce

as many ftieep as may be looked after by; ,one'

person, finds employment for at least five times

as many people, including all the various

for different trades, in common with fiieep or

distincl from them, as well as afford their car-

of what is produced by grazing for the .confu.-

mer, is evidently far superior to thole employ¬

ed in the like preparation of corn. And of

Dublin, Jan. 16. Yesterday being Quarter

day of the guild of merchants, Dublin, the fol¬

lowing resolutions were agreed to:

Rejoined unanimously, That it is not only

the undoubted right, but highly becoming and

of publick utility for all members of a free

Hate, and more especially bodies corporate, to attend to and occasionally declare their sense of

publick measures.

Rejoined unanimously , That it is the duty of

confrituents to instruct their representatives in

every matter of national concern.

Rejoined, That the late sudden prorogation

©f the parliament of this kingdom was un¬

timely, inasmuch as it has impeded the progress

of many new, and prevented the revival of

many old laws, for the benefit, advantage, and

better security of the internal police, commerce,

trade and manufactures of this kingdom.

Rejoined, That this corporation do instrudl

their representatives in parliament on the pre-

fent calamitous situation of this city and king¬

dom, and that such expedients as may be judg¬

ed necessary to prevent the like diftre# here¬

after, be suggested to them for their future

government.

(Signed by order) Ben j. Taylor, Cl. Gd.

TryAris, Dec. 22. A grand council was held

©f the king, at which all the members of the

several stew schemes relative to the finances were

tejcfted, that minister resigned his employ¬

ment the fame evening.

France has declared, that, for the future,

Corsica shall be part of the Gallican church;

and, in pursuance of this resolution, the pope

has granted an rindulto for the nomination of

seven churches in that island. They w r rite

from Avignon, that the king of France has

likewise declared, that the country shall be an-

pexed for the future to Provence, so that it can

never be again separated from the crown.

Rochelle, Dec. 21. A ship belonging to this port lately arrived at the Isle of Re from

Louiiiana, with several persons on board, who are accused of stirring up that Colony against the Spanish government, and were on that ac¬

count arrested by Mr. O’Reilly upon his arri¬

val at New Orleans. These prisoners are, Mr.

Foucault, commissary of the marine, and or-

dppnateur of Louifiana, Mr. de la Freniere,

who was attorney-general of the superior coun¬

cil, ar.d nine other officers and merchants. A

Spanish ship is likewise expected soon with

more prisoners, who have been taken up on the fame account.

Although it has been objected in

The peasant, as u he fide-long lays

having duly fown our subsistence, no

less duly reaps it, and iafely ciepofites

to quicken his fenfibility or enlarge his

poses; but that as the spirit so the

understanding of a man is in him ; and

he ought to be honoured and elleemed

for being no more than what his con¬

dition requires.

The lawyer, skilled in all the arts of

IV.,

O for a thought lb meanly bafe!

Th’ ungrateful youth shall fureiy find

The heart that couih admire his face,

The judicious reader will easily perceive

the alternate rhyme has given a beauty to the

thought, which the unvarying jingle of the former verification could by no means admit

of 5 yet he will also find, that even this me¬

thod of writing wants a particular something

to make it more pointed and expressive. The

second and last line of every stanza, he will

observe clogged with an unaccountable weight

of syllable $ and though in all probability he

might be induced to think the composition

has a good deal of pretty, he will find very

little of the Jinking about it, or in plain Eng-

lish, though he may find nothing to condemn,

he will meet with nothing to admire.

To remove this inconvenience therefore,

suppose we make one effort more, and try

what effedb the shortning of the second and

fourth line may have.

I.

O Damon, still you strive in vain

A fix’d resolve to move !

My heart, alas ! may feci the pairi.

But scorns the guilt of love.

II.

Is this, ye powr’s, his boasted flame ?

Is this his only end ?

And can his love destroy the fame

His honour should defend ?

III.

Perfidious too like all the rest.

Is faithless Damon grown ?

And can he leek to wound a breast

That beats for him alone ?

IV.

O for a thought so meanly bafe!

Th’ ungrateful youth shall find

That heart that could admire his face.

Can hate him for his mind.

In this specimen of measure, the disagree-

able confonance of the first eight syllables with

thej second line is avoided, and two unnecef-

fary syllables are removed from that line, and the last of every verse; by which means the

length of the first and third have a more plea¬

ding found to the ear, and give an additional

force of point and spirit to every second and

fourth. The reader, upon a slight review,

will find a surprizing difference between all

eights, and eights and fixes} and from the in -

The Roman government gave

A nobility may poffefs the whole,

To the KING’S most excellent majesty.

Under the fame secret malign influence,

of this parliament; for the affs of the legif-

feftwre can no more be valid without a kgal

Rjlprefentatiyes of the people are essential

now arrived. The present House of Com¬

mons do not represent the people. We owe

ftricfions of the laws, for the calling and du¬

It was for this we luocefsfully struggleS un¬

der James the Second ; for this we seated and have faithfully supported your majesty’s family

on the throne.

The people have been invariably uniform -

Under James the Second they complained

removing those evil ministers for ever frona

In vindication of the'protesting aldermen

it was urged, that the Remonstrance was not

a legal aft of the city.

The constitution of London said the pro-

tefters is, in miniature, the counter-part of the constitution of England. The court of

aldermen are its house of lords, the common-

council its commons, the whole body of fre'e-

men the people. The two first aft in a de¬

liberative capacity 3 the whole power of the

latter consists in their election of the two for¬

mer. The livery of London are, compara¬

tively speaking, a new power in the consti¬

tution of the city. They were, by what

means is not certain, called in by the com¬

mon-council, about two centuries and a half

ago, to a share of the election of city offi¬

cers 5 but their exclusive right to elective

powers was not establiftied by law, till the eleventh of George the first.

The common-council are the representa-

tives of all the freemen, of whom the livery

are a part. They have the whole manage¬

ment of the police of the corporation 3 the

e< sole right to fpeal: for their constituents to

the king, lords, and commons,” whenever they think the state of the kingdom, or the

safety of the city, renders the exertion ot that

right necessary.

The livery can only be called together fir

the purposes of election, and the electioft

they

they are summonad for, are expressly men¬

cnly the power of individuals to act and fpealc

for theml'elves. They are not an incorpora¬

ted body; they represent no absent members;

they have no constituents ; their powers and

privileges are confined to certain elections.

Whenever the rights of either of the above

Both houses of parliament waited on his

majesty at St. James’s, with their joint ad-

dress on the iobject of remonstrance, which

was as follows:

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE your majesty’s mod dutiful and faith¬

ful subjects, the lords spiritual and temporal,

and commons of Great Britain, in parliament assembled, having taken into consideration the

address lately presented to your majesty under

tfte title of “The humble address, remon¬

strance, and petition of the lord mayor, aider-

men, and livery, of the city of London in

common hall assembled, ” together with the answer which your majesty was pleased to make to the fame ; think ourselves indispen-

libly obliged, upon this occasion, to express

to your majesty the extreme concern and indig¬

nation which we feel at finding that an ap¬

plication" has been made to your majesty, in

terms so little corresponding with that grate¬

ful and affectionate respect which your majesty is so justly intitled to from all your fub-

jefts, at the same time asperfing and calumni¬

ating one of the branches of the legiftature,

and expressly denying the legality of the pre-

tent parliament, and the validity of it’s pro¬

ceedings,

165

To present petitions to the throne has at all

times been the undoubted right of the subjectS

of this realm. The free enjoyment of that

right was one of the many bieffings restored

by the resolution, and continued to us, in

it’s fullest extent, under the princes of your

majesty’s illustrious house: and as we arc

duly sensible of it’s value and importance, it

is with the deepeft concern that we now fee

the exercise of it so grofsly perverted, by being

applied to the purpose, not of prelervine, but

of overturning the constitution, and of pro¬

pagating doctrines, -which if generally a-

doptedmuft be fatal to the peace of the king¬

dom, and which tend to the subversion of all

lawful authority.

Your majesty, we acknowledge with gra¬

titude, has ever shewn the most tender re¬

gard to the rights of your people, not only in

the exercise of your own power, but in your

care to preserve from every degree of infringe¬

ment or violation the powers intruded to others.

And we beg leave to return your majesty our

unfeigned thanks for the frefti proof you have

now given us, of your determination to per-

severe in your adherence to the principles of the corjstitution.

Permit us also to assure your majesty, that it is with the highest satisfaClion we fee your

majesty exprefting so just a confidence in your people. In whatever unjustifiable exccfies

some few mifgjuided persons may in this in-

stance have been seduced to join, your majesty’s subjects in general are too-sensible of what they owe both to your majesty and t»

your illustrious family, ever to be capable of

approaching your majesty with any other fen-

timents than thole of the most 'entire respect

and affeClion 5 and they understand too well

their own true interests to wiffi to loosen the

bands of obedience to the laws, and of due

subordi nation to lawful authority. We are

therefore fully persuaded that vour majesty’s

people, as well as your parliament, will re-

ject with disdain every insidious suggestion of

those iil-designing men, who are in reality

undermining the public liberty, under the

specious pretence of zeal for it’s preservation j

and that your majesty’s attention to maintain

the liberties of your subjects inviolated, which

you esteem your chief glory, will upon every

occasion prove the fure means of strength to

your majesty, and secure to you that zealous

and effectual support, which none but a free

people can bestow.

His Majesty s most Gracious Anjuver.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

1 RETURN you my thanks for this

very loyal and dutiful address. It is with

great satisfaClion that I receive from my par¬

liament so grateful an acknowledgement of my tender regard for the rights of my subjects.

Be assured, that I shall continue to adhere to

the true principles of our excellent constitu¬

tion;

Ext rail of a Letter from Boston, New-Eng-

land, Jan. 29.

(t At a meeting of the non-importing mer“

chants, &c. at Faneuil-Hall, on Tuesdaylaft,

in order to consider of some means of pu-

nishing those who continue to fell goods

imported from Great-Britain, the sheriff

came into the Hall and acquainted the mo¬

derator, that he had a letter for him from

his honour the lieutenant-governor j and the

committee ordered it to be read v of which the following is a copy:

By the Lieutenant-Governor,

To the people assembled at Faneuil-Hall,

“ I should be culpable if I should any Ion*

ger omit to signify to you my sentiments

upon your proceedings. Your assembling to¬

gether for the purposes for which you profefs

to be assembled, cannot be justifted by any

authority or colour of law. Your going from

house to house, and making demands of the

delivery of property, must strike the people

with terror from your great numbers (even if

it be admitted that it is not done in a tumul¬

tuous manner) and is of very dangerous ten¬

dency.

Such of you who are persons of character,

reputation, and property, expose yourselves

to the consequences of the irregular actions of any of your numbers who have been affem¬

bled together, although you may not approve

of them, and although it may be out of your

power to restrain them.

Therefore, as the represen tative of his ma-

jest-y, who is the father of his people, I must,

from a tender regard to your interest, caution

you : And, as cloathed with authority deri¬

ved trom his majesty, I must enjoin and re¬

quire you, without delay, to separate and

disperse, and to forbear all such unlawful

assemblies for the future, as you would avoid

those evils to which you may otherwise esc*

pole yourselves and your country.

T* Hutchinson.’*

The consideration of the.above-mentioned

paper from his honour, involving in it the

question of the continuance of their meeting,

it was calmly considered 5 after which it was

unanimously voted to proceed to the business

of the meeting, and the following return was made to the sheriff at his request in writing,

viz.

Mr. Sheriff Greenleaf,

« It is the unanimous desire of this body,

that you inform his honour the Lieutenant -

Governor that his address to this hody has

been read and attended to, with all that ^de¬

ference and solemnity, which the message

and the times demand} and it is the unani¬

mous opinion of this body, after serious con¬

sideration and debate, that this meeting is

warranted by law : and they desire you to

inform his honour, that they are deter¬

mined to keep consciences void of offence to¬

wards God and towards man.”

Then the sheriff, desiring to be considered

in the light only of the bearer of his honour’s

letter, withdrew from the assembly. And

then the following resolutions were agreed to.

It is very alarming at this important cri¬

sis, notwithstanding the humane and bene¬

volent treatment that the troops quartered in this city, have received from the colony, and this city in particular, (altho’ we have great

ground to suspecl they are not stationed here

to protect us) that they should be so ungrate¬

ful and insulting to the citizens, as to make

several attempts to blow up and cut down Li¬

berty Pole, which has been ere&ed as a me¬

morial of freedom.

This bafe conduct is an ineonteflible proof,

that they are not only enemies to the peace

and good order of this city, but that they ma-

nifeft a temper devoted to destroy the least

monument raised to shew the laudable spirit

of liberty that prevails among the inhabi¬

tants : and as the fame diabolical spirit will

saturally dispose them to ufe their utmost

endeavours to enslave us, they must be con¬

fidered by all men, who are actuated by a free

spirit of liberty, as enemies, mortal enemies,

to all that is valuable to Englishmen.

Impressed by these considerations, We

Resolved that we will not employ any

soldier on any terms whatever; but that we

will treat them with all that abhorrence and

contempt, which the enemies of our happy

constitution deserve. And whereas many of

them have repeatedly travelled the ftfeets

of this city, • in the night, with arms,

with which they have attempted to, take

the lives of many of the citizens, and notwithstanding made their escape, and eluded

the laws, and passed with impunity: there¬

fore, that the' inhabitants may not for tire

future be insulted, and put in peril of their

lives,

Resolved, That if any soldier fir all be

found ia the night having arms (except centi-

nels and orderly ferj cants) or out of the bar¬

racks after the roll is called, fifth as am even

found without arms, and behave in an in¬

fulting manner, shall be treated as enemies

to the peace of this city: and we do hereby

solemnly engage, to and with each other.

That we will, to the utmost of our power,

ftridlly adhere to the above resolutions, and,

if possible, bring the transgreffors of them

to condign punishment.”

LORENCE, Jan. 27. Such a prodigi¬

ous quantity of fnow has fallen in the neighbourhood of Montepulchiano, that the

poor friars could not receive any succour for

eight days, and had not some humane people

then dug a way to the convent, they must

have periftied with famine, as all their pro-

visions were spent.

W E, your majesty’s most dutiful and

patiently submit to them, can deserve to fuf-

By the fame secret and unhappy influence to which all our grievances have been originally

owing, the redress of those grievances has

been now prevented ; and the grievances them-

selves have been repeatedly confirmed ; with this additional circumstance of aggravation,

that while the invaders of our rights remain

the directors of your majesty’s councils, the

from your majesty’s service—your majesty

having been advised by your ministers to re¬

move from his employment, for his Vote in parliament, the highest officer of the law;

because his. principles iuited ill with theirs,

Your subjects look up with satisfaction

We find ourselves compelled to urge with the greater impbrtunity, this our humble but

The Salique law 1 , by which all fe¬

It is true they excluded the name of

RUSSIA.

A coloflal statue of the famous Peter the

Great is making in Russia, the pedestal of which is to consist of one entire stone, weigh¬

ing, at present, 27,000 quintals. This

enormous mass is already removed several

miles from the quarry, in order for its em¬

barkation on the Neva, by means of which they hope to be able to convey it to Peterf-

burgh.

The reason of the applause thus

given to the looser productions, in pre¬

ference to the chaster compositions of the Drama, is very obvious: an actor

of eminence, whether in tragedy, or

comedy, who wants to appear in a new

character, never considers the goodness

of the play, in which he is to appear,

but the variety of situation, or the

fund of hurpour which may be con¬

tained in a particular part; attentive

therefore only to what will give him-

self an opportunity of filming, he is

wholly regardless whether the author

he receives, is moral, or immoral, cal-

culated to injure, or likely to improve

naturally the oftenest in which they are allowed the greatest reputation—

This however is a very erroneous cus¬

tom ; the stage was instituted for fa-

lutary, not pernicious purposes; not

to support the cause of vice, but to

combat in the defence of virtue, and

it is better to annihilate it entirely,

than to make it a pandar to ffie paf-

fions of a people.

ous writer, we must first consider the of¬

it aflumes a manner so different from

were won. [to glow.

Pleas’d with his guests the good man 1 earn’d

And quite forgot their vices in their woe;

Careless their merits or their faults to scan.

His pity gave ere charity began.

Thus to relieve the wretched was, his pride,

And e’en his failings lean’d to virtue’s fide;

But in his duty prompt at every call.

He watch’d and wept, he pray’d and felt, for all.

And, as a bird each fond endearment tries,

To tempt its new fledg’d offspring to the Ikies;

He try’d each art, reprov’d each dull delay.

Allur’d to brighter worlds, and led the way.

Beside the bed where parting life was laid,

And sorrow, guilt, and pain, by turns dif-

may’d.

Eofton (New-England) March 21. On

Thursday last the great and general court or

assembly of this province met at Cambridge,

when the lieutenant governor made a speech

to the council and house of representatives 5

in which he informs them, he intended to

have met the court on the 10th of January at

Boston; but that by the two last packets:

from England he had received such instruc-

tions/as made it necessary for him to prorogue

it to the 15th instant at Cambridge.

mittee) remonstrated to his honour againffc

proroguing the court from time to time, as an

infraction on the essential rights of that af-

fembly, derived to them by the British con¬

stitution and the royal charter.

fore humbly of opinion, considering the cir-

cumstances of the province, that Iris honour

would run no risque of incurring his majef¬

ty’s displeasure by complying with the request:

of both houses.

loaded.

ing found.

Mrs. Macaulay was born in Kent,

yrealty am afraid is much more than can

as Mr. Pope emphatically expresses

DEBATES of a POLITICAL CLUB.

T HE last number of the Political

Debates w r as closed by the speech

of Mutius Sccevola, in defence of the conduct of admiriiftration with regard to Ireland; but as it did not

flofe the argument upon the question,

we think it necessary to give Caius

Collatinus’s celebrated reply:

Mr. President, hr,

THE noble lord who has so ela¬

borately defended the proceedings of

administration, having laid great stress

upon Poyning’s law, and told us that it is the chief Security of our Superio¬

rity over Ireland, it will not be im¬

proper to reconhder the original mo¬

tion at present before the chair, and to take a review not only of the fa¬

mous law in question, but of the vari¬

ous statutes to which it has given

birth. ' : •'

Though it is universally conceived

at present, hr, that Poyning’s law was

foh-ly intended to be a check upon the

Infh parliament, it is nevertheless

certain, that all the historians who

5

have entered deeply into the policy of

Henry the Seventh’s reign, concur in i

opinion, that it was principally de¬

signed to be a curb upon the chief

governors; the a< 5 l itself expressly di¬

rects, that the bills to be pasted in

Ireland should be certified over , under the great seal of that kingdom, previ¬

ous to their commencement. The in¬

conveniences however arihng from

that regulation, led Philip and Mary?|

to give the Irish privy-council a power,

of transmitting bills during the fitting;

of parliament, but it is remarkable,

that np law whatever makes the least

mention of money bills, or once even

supposes their originating in the coun¬

cil ; on the contrary, the public mo¬

ney was understood to flow only from the representatives of the people, and

a very natural conclusion it was, that

those who submitted to the taxation of

their property, were the pjopereft per-

fons to order the mode of its being

taxed. Poyning’s law was besides twice

suspended, once in the reign of Hen-

. .... ... .... . 0 • - r y

177°* Debates of a

vy the Eighth, and once in his daugh¬

ter Elizabeth’s j so that even in those

early periods, while Ireland was un¬

fettled, and while the religious disputes

of England made the very throne of this kingdom insecure, government by

no means thought the ael of Sir Ed¬

ward Poyning was the palladium of

their authority over the filler nation.

Why government should be of that

opinion, when Ireland is closely rivet-

ted to us by every tie of interest and

inclination, I cannot fee in the leaf!;

unless our ministers are conscious,

that they have either done, or mean

to do, fqmething, which mull necef-

farily forfeit the affections of that

country.

It is urged by the friends of admi-

nistration, that the Irish privy-coun¬

cil have a right of originating money

bills ; I should be glad however to

kno-w at what period, since the com¬

mencement of Poyning’s law, they

once exercised that right; it is surely

very extraordinaiy, that if they pof-

selfed a right of such a nature, that

this should be the first in which they

attempted to exercise it j and it is surely

to the full as extraordinary, that they would differ the originating power

ever fmce the tenth year of Henry the

Seventh, to remain with the com¬

mons, if the commons were not the

people legally intitled to it. The

truth is, the privy-council has the pri¬

vilege of certifying parliamentary bills

from Ireland to this kingdom j but

the privilege of certifying by no means

includes the just authority of origina¬

ting 5 yet even admitting in oppofi-

tion to-the first tonnage and poundage

in the 17th of Henry the Seventh,

the preamble of which particulary

lets it forth as the grant of the com¬

mons, that the privy-council had an

equal right to originate, still the com¬

mons were justified in exerting their

negative, and in no manner violated

the spirit of Poyning’s law, in refu¬

ting the bill, because it did not first

proceed from themselves.-The

language of their conduct is simply

this :—Here are two modes of rai-

fmg money proposed, wffich is the best—by privy-council, or parliament ?

both cannot be pra&ifed at the fame

time, we will therefore pursue the

most eligible, and adopt the parlia¬

mentary as the least inconsistent with

Political Club . 335

the principles of a free constitiition.”

The commons accordingly adopted

that mode, and government took the

money j yet government is dissatis-

fied-why ? why because the Irish

house of commons was felicitous for the subject, and made their loyalty to

the sovereign walk hand in hand with the security of the kingdom. Had the

commons indeed rejected the council

money bill “ because it was their own

exduji-ue right to originate,” there

would have been an opposition, tho’

in my opinion a reasonable one, to the

privy-council, but at present the pro¬

ceedings of the latter are no more im¬

pugned, than the prorogation of the former is supported by the precedent

so repeatedly urged, of Lord Sydney

in the year 1692.

I shall not at this time animadvert,

Mr. Presideirt, on the violation of par¬

liamentary privilege by the chief go¬

vernor, but confine myself to his fe-

cretary’s decaration, that the privy-

council money bill was a fine for the

renewal of parliament. This, fir, is

speaking out with a witness—this is

throwing off the mafk at once, and

confidently telling the subject, that he shall not poffefs his absolute right, un-

lefis he pays the minister for indulg¬

ing him with it. Sir, this is oppref-

fion, this is despotism in the extreme^

and as this assembly has a coercive au¬

thority over British ministers in every part of the British dominions, I trull

we shall give the people of Ireland that redress which their own parlia¬

ment cannot grant, and that our in¬

terest will even lea-d us into those mea-

fures which are evidently dictated by

our justice.

Here the debate terminated upon

Irish affairs, but the motion was re¬

jected by 140 against 66.—It is now

necessary to relate the proceedings of the upper club-room on the famous

bill of Victor Americanus, for rever-

fmg the various parliamentary adju¬

dications relative to the Middlesex

election. This bill having been read,

it was supported by some, and object¬

ed to by orhers : the principal speakers

however, were Victor Americanus,

Horatius Tullius (L. M—— d) and

Sulpicius Strabo (L. C-n) the first

in answer to the arguments of a ftre-

nuous objector, thus defended his bill.

Most

334

Most illustrious L—ds,

THE noble lord who last favour¬

ed us with his sentiments, has been

very violent against the present mo¬

tion j he feeras even to be angry with the advocates for the bill, but his an¬

ger is of a species, that must rather

excite our smiles, than provoke our

resentment; I shall therefore take no

notice of the reflexions which he has

thrown out upon the fa£tion as he

politely stiles the minority, but pro¬

ceed at once to recapitulate the cause

of this unlucky measure, which is so

unfortunate as to be the obje<ft of his

indignation.

The great bafis of public freedom in this country, most illustrious 1 —ds,

is the constitutional right which the

lhbjedft enjoys, of eledfting his repre-

fentative into parliament. This right

has been recently and notoriously vio¬

lated by the members of the lower

club, who, though themselves delega

ted, presume to appoint their own

members, and claim the exercise of a

power, even superior to that of the

very people from whom alone they

derive all their authority.—The coun¬

ty of'Middlesex, most illustrious 1 —ds,

lately chose a gentleman, no way in¬

capacitated by the law of the land, to

be their representative; the number of

voices which polled for this gentle¬

man were 3143; against him appears

a court candidate with 296 votes j yet

notwithstanding the great majority in

favour of the former, the lower club-

room not only refuse to admit him,

but actually appoint his opponent to

the vacant feat, in defiance of all law,

in defiance of all shame, in defiance of

all the execrations of their indig-

nant countrymen. If a procedure of this nature is tolerated, what becomes

of every franchise which we hold fa-

cred as Englishmen ? This is laying

the axe at once to the root of our

eonstitution 5 and arguing in extenu¬

ation of it is only adding insult to

injury, and desiring us to kifs the hand

of the assassin, while he mercilefsly

plunges a dagger in our hearts.

It is true the lower club-room had

a right, if petitioned by their self-

appointed member, to examine care¬

fully into the legality of the 1143

votes given for his competitor j but if

the votes were legal they had no right

to let him aside 3 the fame' law that

July

constitutes the lower club-room, gives

the freeholders their discretional power

of chusing whom they please, and it is

to this very power, that the men thus

trampling on the eonstitution, are

indebted for their own political ex¬

istence. But when no petition is

lodged, when no illegality in the

3143 voices is even so much as pre¬

tended, the outrage becomes aggrava¬

ted in proportion to its audacity, and

Shews us that we are not to be allow¬

ed the mere shadow of a eonstitution.

It has been in lifted, that there is

no precedent for this assembly’s ta¬

king notice of the proceedings in the

lower club-room, yet I am pretty po-

fitive, that in the case of Titus Oates,

there is one perfectly in point,

where the lower room took cogni¬

zance of our proceeding. However

the justice of the measure is superior

to the force of precedents, and indeed

if the three branches of the legifla-

ture were not intended as checks upon

each other, we might as well be go¬

verned by one despotic head, and as

well be Haves to one arbitrary master.

It is however said, most illustrious

1—ds, that a spirit of discontent has

gone abroad, and that consequently

the present bill is inexpedient. Now,

for my own particular part, I consider

this objection as a frefti argument in

support of the expediency. If the

nation is discontented, it is our duty

to remove, as far as poftible, this dis¬

content. But our humane ministers,

while they fcaster oppression round

their country, will not even allow the

injured a right of complaining.-

Their majority in the lower club-

poorn is a political inquisition, with which they terrify every orthodox pro-

feft'or of liberty, so that one cannot

help exclaiming with Shakespeare jie *

on their room : i

“ Fie on it ! Oh fie !

“ Tis an unweeded garden, things

“ Rank and grofs in nature poflels it

merely.”

I am apprehensive, I am too appre-

hensive, that this mode of proceeding

springs near the palace 5 but I hope it

will be speedily seen there in all its

genuine deformity. For myself, tho'

I shall never abet the clamours of fac¬

tion, I will ever stand forth an advo¬

cate for the just rights of the people;

and while I am able to crawl upon the

Debates of a Political Club.

Mr. Ariftarchus,

T appears to me that you have

shamefully endeavoured to impose

upon the public, by a false and scan-

dalous letter, in which you, in the

most malignant manner, attack the

as a writer.

Now, Mr. Ariftarchus, I leave you,

ed falsehood. I have turned to the account given of the above-mentioned

while they candidly acknowledge his

viewers, you will do well to shew

am, Mr. Ariftarchus, as much as an.

honest man ought to be,

Your humble Servant,

“ My lords.

This is an information for a [edition?

printing and publishing of a paper

signed Junius : The jury have found

Mr. Woodfall guilty of printing and publishing only.

<e (1.) I shall first contend, that this is

an acquittal. The charge brought

3S7

before the juiy is grounded upon the defendant’s evil and seditious design in

publishing. The jury find the publish-

ing only. This then is not convi&ing

him of the charge } which is, the fe¬

ditious intention. It is first necessary to prove upon the trial the faft of pub¬

lication ; next the construfHon put

upon the paper in the information.

These. are the points which are to be given in charge to the jury ; and the jury must be convinced of both. By

the general word of guilty, the jury

find the whole charge to be true. They

have not done so. They have not found

the fa< 5 t of publication merely ; but they have added negative words, to exclude

every thing else. To what the jury

do not fay, there is by law a nega¬

tive. f But here the jury have them-

selves taken care, that their silence

shall not be mifinterpreted. Had they

been silent, whether the paper was a

libel or not, and not referred it to the

opinion of the court, their silence must

have acquitted ; but here they have

ufedthe word only, expressly to exclude

every idea of a crime.

If juries may be justly said to nega¬

tive every thing they do not find, in

a question of civil property, much

more must they be said to do so now,

where the criminal motive makes the offence they have in charge, I do not

fay, that a strict and literal proof must be brought of every part of the infor¬

mation ; but I do fay, that criminal

intention is of the eflence of a crime,

and must enter into every idea of guilt.

Of this criminal intention the jury are the judges \ and if they exclude that the defendant is acquitted.

To support a general verdict of guil¬

ty, it must appear that the jury believ¬

ed the paper libellous. Whether li¬

bellous or not depends only upon the

construition put in the information.

This construflion they have excluded

therefore, though they have not said

a libel, they have negatived the libel-

ling construcftion, and said as rr\uch in

Lijft of all the name of Richard Oliver, efq.

was called over, when there was a general

red by the sheriffs duly elected with the louo-

eft acclamations. Mr. Oliver then came for¬

wards, and addrefied himself to the livery in

a speech on theoccasion.

“ Favoured as I have been, and now ho¬

noured by you, gentlemen of the livery, my

words cannot sufficiently express my ferati-

ments of gratitude for your early and as yet

unmerited confidence reposed in me by the

choice you have unanimously made of me as

your representative in parliament. To your

general and warm support it is owing that I

have not had an opponent ; and this circum-

flance is most pleasing to me, becauleit proves

that your spirit is not to be influenced or over¬

ruled whenever you think proper to unite in

the free exercise of your rights.

I wish, gentlemen, that I had already given

you any proofs that I shall not abuse the trust

you have placed in me ; hut as I have not yet

fat in parliament, accept my assurances atpre-*

font, that I will ever consider myself as depu-I

ted by you for your benefit, and not for my

own advantage : that as, in the course of my

life I never have received or desired, so,

whether I have the honour to continue an al¬

derman and representative of this city or not,

I never will accept, directly or indire&ly,

either place, pension, emolument, contract,

or gratification of any kind whatever, from the crown or its ministers. My foie motives

of publick conduct shall be the advance¬

ment of the publick welfare, and the rea-

fonable honest hope of your approbation,

free from every other influence or considera-

tion. I shall he obedient to the instructions

you have a right to' give to the servants you ap¬

point. I will contribute my ftiure in any

manner to rtyider justioe to the freeholders

1770.' 5 The MONTHLY CHRONOLOGER. 383

of Middlesex, and In them to all the other

counties and boroughs in Great-Britain, for the injury they have all received by being un¬

lawfully and most dangerousiy deprived of a

representative in parliament, who has been

duly and repeatedly eletted by those who alone

have and ought to have the right of eledcion.

I am confident, gentlemen, that your only

security against the abuse of that power, which

you intrust to your representatives, must be a

frequent appeal to you by shortening the dura¬

tion of parliament: by an effective, not a

nugatory place and pension bill : by an ade¬

quate and true representation throughout he

kingdom. For either and all of these securi-

tics to the people my vote shall moll chearful-

ly be given, arid my endeavours most ftrenu-

oufiy employed whenever the happy time

comes (and through the persevering virtue of

you, my fellow citizens, it mult come) that

these essential points can be obtained.—I will

ufe my utmost endeavours to remove the just

complaints of America, which operate to

your present diladvantage in a commercial con¬

nexion, as well as in a political view } for the fame system of injustice and despotism, if

established against the Americans, will be exercised towards you 5 and the principles of

fair government forbid that they should be

taxed without representation, ,as much as that the people of this country should pay taxes to which, or to the continuance of which they have not consented.

I will endeavour, gentlemen, to the utmost

of my abilities to aift up to the station in which you have placed me. My life will be

happily employed if I shall ever be able to

render you services in any measure equal to

those of your late much-lamented representa¬

tive, whose memory will be dear to me, as it

is to every good citizen : but though I should

fail in these vvifhes, I can at least promiseyou

in full confidence that I will equal him in

the integrity of his heart, and in the inde¬

pendence of his spirit.”

AIR.

See ! the Lark unfolds his wings,

Swiftly foars, and sweetly lings;

Thro’ the Ikies his mu lie floats,

Distant hills vibrate the notes.

Feather’d fongfters on each fpray.

Roll tranflucent streams along.

Old Oceanus peaceful lies,

Ting’d with rofeate dappled Ikies,

His heid waves in wanton play;

The vail: expansion murm’ring sweep:

While smoothly glides the wat’ry way.

A I R.

Thus August displays to our fight.

Bright Phrebus in golden array.

Unveiling his filler Delight,

And calling her forth to the day.

All nature expressive of Love,

The mind’s sympathetic sweet theme.

Rich Ceres appearing in view,

Content and young Peace in her train.

By the accounts of the late earthquake at

an hundred families, two leagues from Port-

au-Prince, wholly funk and disappeared,

number of people in it, was intlantly taken in by r the opening of the earth, so that no

mountain, Handing close by the shore, was

thrown into the fea, which caused a swell to

the height of 130 feet above the common

surface. Another large mountain, about

two miles from Port-au-Prince, was blown up

in the air, leaving in its place a bason of wa¬

ter about three or four fathoms deep.

Cr other articles, on which a duty is enabled,

as the condition upon which the people here

signed for the proposed alteration, was that

Boston and Philadelphia approved and came

into the measure, their refusal puts an end to

the measure proposed, so that the non-im¬

portation agreement remains in full force,

and doubtless will continue so tiil the end is

obtained. '

rent, and in a quarter of an hour the water,

rofe ten feet : seventeen houses were, throw*

neeeffiary in such a calamity.

“ The letter which I had the honour to

along the Pruth, cppOfite the body of our

which they strengthened oa every

fide with a prodigious quantity of cannon.

Notwithstanding their situation (which was

of numbers) we resolved, on the 28th ult.

used all our diligence, we were not able t©

re*oh them till the 15th inft. when we found

toons to the number of twenty thousand, who

made a /hew of .attacking our front, but were

The deserters and prisoners all confirm,

that the Turkish army was commanded by

Caplan Ghieri, Chan of Crimee, who, con¬

three bachas, named Jftnael, Abafa, and

thousand men. Notwithstanding their ad¬

vantageous situation, I resolved to come to a

decisive engagement, which began at day¬

break on the 18th, and ended in a most

complete viftory on our fide j for as soon as -

our men had gained the fumroit of the moun¬

tain, they drove the enemy out of four in-

whole extensive camp, and an imrnenfe

quantity of all forts of ammunition and pro-

visions, together with thirty-eight pieces of

fine brass cannon, and a great number of co¬

lours.”

HIS infamous scheme

4 f now failing, and ad-'

to fapport the legal

authority of the mo-

ry part of her dominions } a com¬

plaint is now brought before this af-

fembly of our misconduct, our inca¬

pacity, our oppression; the parlia¬

ment of England is now told of our

delinquency, and called upon to pu-

nish our malverfations 5 yet how has

government offended? Is the legifla-

ture of this kingdom to punish us for

maintaining its own supremacy ? Are

the people of England to execrate us,

because we have particularly ltood

forth against every effort of faction,

to secure them in the possesslon of

their dependencies ? I will not, my

1—s, insult your understandings, I

will not insult the virtue of the na¬

tion, to suppose it. Let our patriots

therefore, if they would arrive at

eminence by their conduct, go over

to America, and defnand the confi¬

dence of the colonies. They may have real merit to plead there in

their attempts to overturn the con-

•istitution of Great-Britain; they may have merit there , by endeavouring to

jrender the impudent resolutions of a

provincial committee, superior to our

lawful ordinances.-But here, 1

trust they will be ever held con¬

temptible} that their clyaradters will

be as mean, as their proceedings

have been flagitious, and that their

machinations to destroy the impor¬

tance of the English empire, will

Sept. 1770.

always make them detestable to every

good Englishman.

The %voidd-be patriots, my l—s,

who have paraded so much upon their

public spirit, are exceedingly offended

with the military, and declaim very

pompously on the outrages which they committed in Bolton. But fare-

ly it is not criminal in any subject,

whether a soldier or not, to defend

his life legally, when it is illegally at¬

tacked. The Bolton accounts them-

feives, acknowledge the townsmen to

be the aggressors, and is a soldier to

be particularly exposed to the licen-

fioufness of the rabble, because he

is performing his duty ? or is he

to be less intitled to protection than

another man, because he is more

immediately than any other man, de<«

voted to the fervlce of the commu¬

nity ? God forbid. Fashionable foever

as it may be to condemn our troops,

for supporting the due execution of the laws, and aiding the necessary au¬

thority of the civil magistrate, I still

trust that justice will triumph over

clamour : I still trust that reason will

maintain its proper pre-eminence over

faction, and that this house will not

consider those popular worthies, much

intitled to its thanks, for publickly im¬

peaching its constitutional jurisdiction.

A noble D—~— has been pleased to

call my letter to fame of the Ame¬

rican governors, directing a diffolu-

tion of their respective assemblies, ill-

written , and anti-constitutional , wanting

the fandtion of parliamentary advice,

as well as the mildness of justifiable

authority.

I will not, my 1—ds, venture to

Hand up in defence of my letter as a

piece of composition; I am not vain

enough to flatter myself with an idea

of literary excellence, nor presump-

tuous enough to suppose any produc¬

tion of mine, would be able to defy

the ordeal of his grace’s criticism. But

with regard to the meaning of my

hand upon my heart, and not only

acknowledge the motive, but glory

in it. It may perhaps be criminal in

the- eyes of that noble D-—« to

Delates cf a Political CmIk

vindicate the fu^emacy of the mother

country r and it may in his opinion

claim the applause of the people by

sacrificing their rights, and pay his

court to this illustrious house, by dis¬

puting the legality ot its ordinances.

For my part, being in office, I can

have no pretence to these exalted

inconfiilencies, which lo peculiarly

discinguish the flame of modern pa-

triotism. Plain common lenfe is the

only advocate I shall attempt to em¬

his grace point out in what : if it is

dictated by severity, let him shew us

in what the severity confirts. Ir in¬

deed it is repugnant to the principles of the Britifli conflitution to execute

the laws of Great Britain, I am a cul¬

prit of the first magnitude. If it is

oppression to diii'olve those provincial

Nor do I wonder, when it is public vir¬

that it should be held criminal to ap¬

pear in their defence. My criminali¬

ty however is my principal boast.—

The star of America shall never

have my voice, to Ihme either upon the destrublion or the diigraqe of Eng-

tiihmen.—The colonies are our fub-

je£ts —as such they are bound by our

the language of supplication, to beg

that our subjeSis wjll c ondefcendingly

It is a mighty argument with po¬

pularity, my 1 — s, that govern¬

concise the unhappy disputes betwesn

Sept.

cans, and the inability to else£I that

deflreable reconciliation, is constantly

and then they exclaim, because our

<D

us. In fabt, my 1—s, their whole

every bait must be throwm out to

tented : so they can succeed to office,

lic good. This poor kingdom may

be sacrificed to her dependencies,

and the Britifli parliament be redu¬

THOUGH some noble person-

ages, who are connected with govern¬

ment, seem anxious for a speedy de¬

termination of the present question,

and though others have called out to

adjourn, I think it my duty to fay a

few words, notwithstanding the great-

ness of their impatience, and I hope

they will not so far impeach the rec¬

titude of their own measures, as ta¬

citly to confess they will not bear an

examination.

The noble 1 —d, who has now fa¬

voured us with his defence, is pleated

to be very severe upon the gentlemen

in opposition, and to attribute their

endeavours for the public welfare, to

a mean desire of getting into office.

I do not, however, fee why they are

to be branded with a ltigma of this

nature, any more than the noble 1 -d

himself; they are as independent in

their fortunes, as upright in their

principles as his 1--p, and have

less temptation, surely, by the mere

hope of being employed, to prejudice

their country, than his lordship, who

is actually in place, and may be rea-

fonably supposed no way desirous of

quarrelling about trifles, either with the influences he consequently pof-

fefles, or the emoluments.

It is universdly allowed, however

we may censure the conduct of the

Americans, that the fint exercise of a

power to tax them in the parliament of this country, was at leaf extremely

i injudicious, if it was not even actually

illegal, since much more was to be

eot from their affection than their

fear, from the extenflon of their com¬

merce than the increase of their pub¬

lic burdens. While they submitted

therefore to regulate their commerce

by our diferetion, they thought it

hard that their property fltould also be

at our disposal, and that we should

not only reflrain them in the acqui/l-

tion of this property, but apply it

•when acquired, to answer our own

exigencies. They contentedly pursu-

ed tflefe paths to obtain their little

wealth, which we judged moil con¬

ducive to our interest, but they denied

our right of taking aw ay that w ealth

'•when 'obtained, and of trrifling to the

diferetion of any authority, what they

naturally enough considered to apper¬

tain wholly to themselves. It was of

course no way wonderful, that in op-

poflng what they deemed a palpable '

invafton of every thing dear, they

ftiould fly to some excefles, The mo¬

ther country herself, upon particular

cccafions, is not able to restrain the

w here they have apparently less foun¬

dations for complaint. She should

Universal experience demon Urates,

When I talk of the myilerious

I am aware that my proposition,

Ajaccio in Cornea, from whence ahe brought

51 of the banditti of that island, who have

Surrendered themselves to the clemency of the king. The colonel of the regiment of Pro¬

vence, who headed some piquets, made this

rapture at Orta, in the province of Tico, on

the other fide the mountains. They were

conducted to the great tower, and one of

their chiefs, named Benedetto, is among

boats which arrive weekly here have come

without some prisoners. The great tower is

the place where they are confined, and they are afterwards fent to the Ifie of Rhe, from

whence they are transported to America. It

is certain if this method is continued, that

Corsica will in zo years be peopled by a new

race. No greater regard is paid to the clergy

than to the laity, several religious of different

communities having been fent to France.

While the parliaments of France, with all

the vigour of great and liberal minds, are op-

posing the tyranny of the court in the affair

of the Duke d’Aiguillon, the dependants of the crown are enforcing the will of their so-

vereifn with all the arbitrariness of an eastern

monarch, and all the violence peculiar to

mean and little fouls, fn. Britanny two of the members have been banished by letters de

cachet. At Metz, Marshal d’Armentieres

panies of grenadiers, and after tearing to

pieces an arret of that parliament, banished

several of the members to Vizoul. .The par¬

liament of Befancon having committed the king’s attorney tjiere into confinement, Mar-

shal de Lorges, commandant of Franche

Comte, went at the head of a detachment,

and forced open the prison, and fet the attor¬

ney at liberty. In this manner things are

going on between the parliaments and the court $ but as the parliament of Paris still

continues its representations with vigour, and

all the other parliaments seem to partake of

•he fame spirit, it is not impossible but the court may find itself at last obliged to recede.

broke out in Podolia and Volhinia, and it is

assured that our court has fent orders to rein¬

force the line of troops upon the frontiers,

and to double the quarantine. There is no

doubt of every precaution being taken to

prevent the spreading of that diilemq-vr, but

affairs; 49 i

will likewise find it very difficult to escape

fable communication which the carrying oft*

provisions occasions.

Vienna, Aug; 14. It is difficult to con¬

ceive how r the waters of the Danube come to

be so high as they are at present, when they

used to be so low',' especially after so hot and

dry a season as we have had for some time

past, and without' any rain. They are so

prodigiously swelled, that they broke loose a

large raft, which being carried down by the

current, struck against an arch of our grand

bridge,, and demoiished it with a most ter¬

ttion was ever so well governed as

Teat Britain is at this moment, and

lat no opposition was ever so in-

Ltn$us, as the opposition which is uni-

erfally made to their administration;

at when the inconteftible evidence of

i£ts, is hourly contradiiting their

toft plausible declarations, we are

oliged to resent the insult offered to

ar understanding, as much as the stab

[redded at our freedom, and to expose

le futility of their arguments, tho’

e despair of any benefit from their

mviition.

The noble i—d who has acknow-

dged himself the oftenfible minister

a the present question, has talked

ry loudly about our rights, yet he

s not (hewn in any manner how

efe rights have been supported either

r himself, or by any other member

the administration ; does it look like

pporting our rights to. shrink from

examination of his own condudd ?

does it look like supporting our

jhts to prevent the enquiries of par-

iment with premature motions of

fljournment ? of what ule is our af-

cmbling, if we are not allowed to ex-

tefs our sentiments ? of what service

l it to recommend any national objedd

1 our attention, if it.is not to be fe-

bufly considered ?—The people—I

ipeat it, are virtually robbed of their

legifiature, if that legislature is not

allowed a power of adding, and the

ministry in vain tell us of supporting

the authority of the mother country

in America, when they divest her of

all constitutional jurisdiction in her

own immediate assemblies.

Here, my 1 —ds, is a business referred

to us by express command from the

throne, perplexed in', its nature, but

highly important in its end.—It is re¬

ferred to us particularly, because it has

already baffled the utmost efforts of

administration. —We accordingly en¬

ter upon it in obedience to the royal

mandate, and in justice to our suffer-

•ing countrymen.—Yet the very power

that fends it to us, and requires our

a’lfiftance, takes it peremptorily out of

our hands before we express the least

opinion ; and for what purpose ? To

lodge it again with the man, that has

declared it too mighty for his abilitiesj

and this very man, to whole mis¬

management the chief complaints are

attributed, has himself the temerity

to move for re-committing it to his

own direction—This is an unprece¬

dented insult to the dignity of parlia¬

ment, and could only be intended to make us feel the omnipotence of the

minister.—Severely therefore we do

feel it, efpeckily as it prevents us no

less from obeying the command of the

f— n, than from consulting the welfare of the people, and throws dil-

honour on the c-n, while it

pours in additional calamities upon the kingdom.—Reduced to a state so

truly deplorable, of what service is it

to appear any longer in the political

theatre, where, at befc, we are treated

with ridicule, and denied every oppor¬

tunity of adding a useful, character for

our country?—Secure in their num¬

bers, our managers rule us at present

These debates in the upper club

room on the bulmefs of America, na¬

turally lead us now to enter upon the

arguments resulting from the motion

of Paulus Prifquinius in the lower af-

fembly, on the fame subject. This

motion was made on the 8th of May,

and introduced in the following man¬

ner by Prifquinius:

Mr. President, Sir,

AS in the royal fpesch the affairs

of America were particularly recom¬

mended to the cohsideration of this house, and as a variety of papers

have been now laid before Us, relative

to the state of his m ——y’s govern¬

ment beyond the Atlantic, I think

W r e are expressly called upon, elpeci-

ally in these critical times, to enquire

how the ministers here, no less than

their officers there , have managed so

unfortunately as to kindle the present

flame of cHfiension between the mother

country and her colonies. In fulfill¬

ing this duty, Mr. President, we

mull not only weigh the matter of

fact , but the right of things ; not on¬

ly the turbulence of the Americans, but

the cause of that turbulence; and not only the power of the crown, but the

equity with which that power has b^en

exercised.

Sir, the. people of New England,

though now labouring more immedi¬

ately under our dif leafure than any other of the colonies, are, to my

knowledge, as well affected to the law¬

ful government of Great-Britain, and

as cordial Well-withers to order, as

the most loyal of their fellow-subjects;

and such till lately was their attach¬

ment to the mother country, that du¬

ring the late burthensome w r ar, they

always anticipated the wishes of our

parliament ; they did not avail to be

asked for their money to support the

common cause ; nor make it necessary to argue them into supplies : on the contrary, they were always ambit-ions

of preventing our demands, and well

convinced I am, that had the famous

French descent by any accident taken place, they would have fent over a

{poritaneous afnftance to reinforce our

operations again ft the daring invaders

of thi kingdom.

I grant, Mr. President, that the Sen¬

timents of the New Englanders are

veiy much changed; but the change

is not their crime ; it is their mis for¬

tune ; they have found their duty re¬

turned with insult; and their attach¬

ment made use of, to treat them with

severity; because they chearfully fub-

mitted to our laws as subjects, we

have wantonly attempted to make

them slaves; and because they allowed

our constitutional right of regulating

their commerce, we have proceeded

to tax their property against the evi¬

dent principles of the constitution.

You fee therefore, fir, that though

the Americans have refitted, they have not refilled the’ just dominion,

but the unwarrantable authority claim¬

ed by the administration of this king¬

dom ; they have not opposed the fu-

premacy , but the violence of our acts;

they are willing to obey every ordi¬

nance which an Englishraan ought to

obe}^; but when we tell them that their lives and properties are to be en¬

tirely at our disposal; when we tell then*

their little wealth must be acquired

just as w 7 e think proper to direct; and

that when acquired, it must be subject to our taxation; they fhudder at the

bare idea of such accumulated oppref-

fion ; they ccnfider us as tyrants, not

as sovereigns, and think themselves

supported by every law of nature, and every argument of reason, to throw

off their subjection when we throw

off our justice.

Justice and allegiance, Mr. Prefi¬

dent, are reciprocal duties ; the one

cannot exist without the other ; and

it was upon this principle our noble

ancestors conduced themselves at the

ever memorable period of the glorious

Resolution. Upon this principle the

colonies are proceeding now ; they find

themselves injured by anti- constitu¬

tional laws, and that instead of.ex¬

pecting their humble Applications

for a repeal of these laws will be in¬

dulged, they are to be dragooned in¬

to submiflion by a military force;

they fee that acquiescence, is as fatal^

as opposition, and that either fide of the alternative is pregnant with de-

Itruction ; yet as Engii'hmen they fee

which is the propereft to chufe, death

or chains, a grave or dishonour; they

therefore prefer the first to the lalt,

and are the more confirmed in their

choice

■V) 7°‘

choice, when they recollect that their

ilavery is not intended for the benefit

of the mother country, but to grati¬

fy the avarice, or glut the revenge of

an arbitrary ministry.

The establishment of a military force, in the present manner, thro'

the American colonies, though said

to be established for supporting the

due execution of the laws, is in itfejf

a flagrant aft of injustice ; because the power is wrested from the hands

of the civil, to be lodged entirely

with a military officer. Military go¬

vernments are repugnant to the very

idea of freedom; they are a serpent

in the boiom of the constitution, and the more they are cherished, the more

deadly we shall find their sting. Be-

fides, Mr. President, every military

power which the crown had a right

to grant, is granted to the governor and council of the various colonies:

there is a solution desired to the

asmuch as the Father exalted him to

“ A courier that lately arrived in eight,

Russians had been for some time straitened in

resolved to leave Bender blockaded, and to make a vigorous puflr with the main army in¬

to a more fruitful and hea-lthful country;

they therefore struck their tents, and began

their march towards Constantinople. This,

as might be expected, alarmed the Divan.

Four baffas of three tails were immediately

dispatched with orders to risque a general en¬

gagement. The old vizier, who had hitherto

commanded the Turkish army, at fight of this order funk into clefpair, alledging, that

as the Russians were now far distant from,

their own country, nothing more was re¬

quired for their destruction, but to cut off

their convoys, break up the ways before

them, harafs them with mock attacks, and

wait till winter should do the rest. The Baf¬

fas toid him that their orders were perempt¬

ory, and that he must fight, or resign to

those who had greater courage. The vizier

replied, that he was willing to die, though

he was not willing to fight: that he would

lead on the army, and as he was resolved

never to live to apologize for his defeat, he-

charged them to remember and report his

opinion.

The two armies met upon a kind of pa-

n infill a, formed by a confluence of the

Neifter and the. Danube.; The dispute was very bloody, and the event for some time

doubtful. They, began, as is the present

custom, by a dreadful fire of tire artillery,

during- which the vizier’s horse was fwe.pt

from under him, and the left-hand of Ge¬

neral Rotczinfky carried away. The mala

battle soon joined, and the impression made by the jamffaries, who, throwing away their

mufquets, charged with their feymetars, was

so dreadful and violent, that if they had been well seconded by the Spahis and Tartars,

there, is reason to believe they would have

gained the day. The first line of the Ruf¬

lians was broken, and fell back in disorder

upon the second. The jamffaries preflc.d on

with fayage clamour, but in the ardour of

fucccfs relaxed their ranks.;, while the Ruf¬

fian right wing having encountered and dif-

perfed 20,000 Tartars, wheeled round upon

their backs, and obliged them to make two

fronts to oppose the Russian foot on one side,

and their horse on the other. Justi.ce re¬

quires us to declare that the janifiarics, thus

surrounded, defended themselves with unex¬

ampled bravery, but the number of their

enemies was too great. The} were at last

overwhelmed, and the vizier died in his post

according to his prediction.

rished in the Neifter, and some in the Dan-

“ The north-eastern parts of Europe are at

^refe nt both delighted and terrified by a fpe-

cies of magnificence with which the world

has been for some time unacquainted. The

Grand Seignor has at last taken the field in

person. He is the only Turkish emperor

•who has headed his own armies since the

time of Solyman the magnificent. When

notice was given in the feraglio that an im¬

perial camp was to be formed, it may easily

be conceived what was the surprife, and what

was the tumult. As all the preparation was

new, every officer of the household had some-

thing to do which he had never done before,

and which therefore he knew not how to do.

It was observed that the Grand Seignor, who,

through all the accidents of this war, hadpre»

served a natural or affected tranquillity, came

out of his harum solicitous and dejedled, hav¬

ing been, as it is supposed, ruffled by the oil-

order of the women and their attendants, of whom some were weeping and fainting, be-

cause they, were felefted for the march, and others furicus and clamorous, because, being

left behind, they thought themselves neglect¬

ed. But in the courts of eafiern princes,

fear and resentment are idle passions. The

order of the mailer must be obeyed. The

Grand Seignor sets out with a pomp becom¬

ing what he ftvles himself, the mailer of the

That no encouragement may however be

Be it known to the invincible defenders

An Essay on the landed Interejl.

A N D is, in itself, of little or no

value to the owner. The folita-

fy lord of a million of acres would be

but a naked, defenceless and miserable

creature, deflitute of every conveni¬

ence and bleiling of life. A landed

man’s commodity, therefore, derives

^11 its value from the commodities of

others : such as the labour of the huf-

bandman, the skill and toil of thearti-

zan, the industry and property of the

dealer (who purchases, like all other

people, the products of lands for con-

fumption) and the wealth and know¬

ledge of the merchant, who exports

them.

Experience has long shewn that a

people, by their skill and industry,

.may become rich, powerful and happy

without the possession of lands for agri¬

culture 3 because money will procure

a fure supply of such products, from

other countries. But land, without

.people, is of no value at all. Why,

therefore, all power should be assumed

by, and all preference in consideration

.fee given to the possessors of land, in

,jl

any country, is an enquiry worth

making ; but more especially in a tra¬

ding nation, like ours. Yet such has

really become the case, from making a

landed qualification necessary for ob¬

taining a feat among the representa-

tives of the people 3 and, in moil in¬

fiances, from having landed debtors,

or such as are under the influence of

men of landed property.

Hence has arisen the distinction of a

•landed interest 3 which has become

paramount in its operations, from in-

gro-iling all influence in the hate, and

ail weight in the scale of interests 3 > at

ieaft in comparison with theirs who give

to land its whole value. And hence

too has arisen the partial favour which

we fee shewn to that kind of property,

by giving a more than natural value to

the products of lands 3 to the injury of the state, the hurt of our national trade*

and the prejudice of the people. But

this is a point that will hereafter be

more fully considered and explained.

An Fffay on the monied or trading Interest,

T H E interest of traders, like that

of landed men, is to make the

moll they can of their commodities,

which are skill, industry and money 5

being each of them separately, or all

together, a man’s property : but they have no means, like landed men, to

give them an artificial value. These

commodities are generally employed

four distinct ways 3 which are manu-

Causes of the spreading of the Plague.

Several causes contributed to spread the

Infection. The first was, Fear, which

disposed the Body to receive the Contagion,

and gave it a greater Power, where it was received; for Fear lessens, if not destroys the

Influence of the vital Motions^ weakens the

Constitution, sinks the Spirits, and renders

the Geconemy less liable to refill Putrefac¬

tion. This is confirmed by People who,

through Dread or Conceit, have received the

Small-Pox. Several were so frightened by the

Distemper as to die, away on the Spot, and others loft their Senses, Memory, and Un-

derstanding. A second cause was the in¬

credible Number of Inhabitants in the City

and Suburbs, computed to be above 100,000

more than it had ever entertained before,

consistiag of disbanded Soldiers, Court De¬

pendants, ruined Loyalists, Tradesmen from the Country to fettle, and a vast Number of

Workmen, Manufacturers, &c. (of whom

alone the Ribband-Weavers were estimated

at 100,000) tofupply the Luxury and Gaiety

both of the City and Court. A third Caule

going through the Streets into Shops and

Markets, it was impoftible for them to avoid

distempered Persons, who conveyed the fatal

Preservatives, Preventions, and

Remedies used.

First ; Dogs and Cats, who were capable

of carrying the Effluvia or infectious Steams

in then Fur or Hair, were ordered to be

destroyed, which was done to the Number

of 40,000 Dogs and five Times as many Cats.

Secondly j Fne best Method to prevent

the spreading of the Infection is to remove-

the well from the diseased 5 and if that can¬

not be practised, to remove the diseased to

cleanly and airy Habitations, out of all great-

Towns, iupplying them with proper Provi-

fions  and Necessaries. Thirdly; The

keeping Preservatives in the Mouth and

about the Clothes, repelled and kept out the

Intention : 1 hofe who used them were lefa

exposed, their Houses were not so furiously

attacked, and thouiands of Families were

by that Means preservd. Fourthly; A

grand Prefer vative is the holding Garlick

and Rue in the Mouth, and smoaking Tobac¬

co, which preservd the Sexton of St. Stei

phens s, Coleman-street, from the Infection,

Fifthly; Pest-H®uses, of which there were only two, were a great Preservative,
